title: Start Here
one_liner: The plain-language front door: what We The Citizens is in sixty seconds, and then in five minutes. No vocabulary a newcomer has not met yet, no award arithmetic, no acronyms — just what this is, what it fixes, who it is for, and the one thing to do next.
scope_in: What the movement is; what problem it exists to fix; who it is for; the one-sentence and one-paragraph versions; a map of the rest of this site; and the single call to action to app.WeTheCitizens.io.
scope_out: Any mechanism detail — how awards are computed, how evidence chains work, how trust is scored. Those get linked from here, never explained here.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What is this, and why should I care?

title: The Problem
one_liner: What is actually broken, stated without jargon and without asking the reader to already agree. Representative democracy is not delivering what it promised, officials are too often captured by money and by interests that are not the voters, and a citizen who notices has had no instrument for establishing it — only argument, which changes nothing.
scope_in: Representative democracy not working as promised; the capture of institutions by money and by interests that are not the citizen base; the deliberate-deadlock pattern — classify a slice of the record, block its recovery, then demand 100% proof before anyone may speak; and why arguing on social media changes nothing.
scope_out: Our answer to it — that is how_it_works. Naming specific living people — that lives in the politician areas, under the sourcing rules.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Why does anything need fixing?

title: Congress Working For Citizens
one_liner: The question every other area on this site serves. Is Congress and the federal government actually working for US citizens, or has control over them been hijacked — by money in politics, by a globalist deep state, by an intelligence service, or by any other power that is not the citizen base? This area is the whole arc: how capture is detected, how it is proven from the official record rather than asserted, how it is exposed once proven, and how the control is finally removed.
scope_in: The ways control gets hijacked — money in politics, a globalist deep state, an intelligence service, or any other power that is not the citizen base; what capture looks like in the public record; how it is detected and proven rather than argued; how it is exposed once proven; and how the control is actually removed, which on this site always means an election.
scope_out: The evidence files behind any one capture — those are problems. The named people who let it happen — those are the politician areas, and every claim there is sourced to the official record.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Who is Congress actually working for?
source_section: 1.0 Making sure Congress and Government is working for US Citizens

title: Why A Non-Partisan Site
one_liner: Why WeTheCitizens.io deliberately takes no side. Some capture is egregious enough that it runs against the base of both parties at once, and the formal party apparatus in Washington has not fixed it in either. This door is the shared ground where citizens from every party can look at the same record, reach a decision together, and then go carry it back into their own party's door.
scope_in: Why a non-partisan door exists alongside the four party doors; what only becomes visible once you stop arguing party — capture that damages Republicans, Democrats, Libertarians and Democratic Socialists alike; the cross-party citizen forum for deciding when the DC party apparatus has failed to fix the problem; and where a visitor goes next once they want their own party's version.
scope_out: Every partisan issue and every partisan instrument — party plans, party laws and fix bills, the board of directors, the yearly strategic conference, the political-spectrum vote that matches you to candidates, trust-score voting, and any religious framing. All of those live only on the four .com doors, and the .io names none of them as its own.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Why is this site not taking a side?
source_section: 2.0 Non-Partisian Site

title: The Movement
one_liner: Who We The Citizens is and what joining actually means — the charter, the four pillars, and an honest answer about what it costs. The same name covers the company, the movement and the software, and it is a tool rather than a service: the whole thing runs without an account, without your real name, and without anyone's permission.
scope_in: The charter and the vision; the four pillars in plain language; the two personas the product serves, citizen and admin; what membership costs and does not cost; the paid-supporter option; and how decisions inside the movement itself get made.
scope_out: Product mechanics, which are how_it_works; and the paired social network, which is covered under repos.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Who is behind this, and what am I joining?

title: How It Works
one_liner: The core loop, end to end. Record your positions and run the calculation; compare the result against the social contract; record where they do not line up; have the AI re-check the logic from first principles rather than from authority; cast your fix; and publish it if you want to. The same loop runs for one citizen alone and for a community of thousands.
scope_in: The six-step loop; individual mode versus community mode at a glance; what the app does for you and what it deliberately never does for you; and a worked walkthrough of one real issue from first question to cast fix.
scope_out: Install steps, which are get_started; and the internals of any single pillar, each of which has its own area.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What do I actually DO with it?

title: Get Started
one_liner: Two ways to run We The Citizens, and they are the same software: hosted at app.WeTheCitizens.io, or local-first on your own computer at localhost:4444. On your own machine there is no account, no server, and nothing leaves the box unless you decide to send it.
scope_in: Hosted versus localhost:4444; choosing your mode on first run; the movement data repo and why the app asks for it; signing in, which is optional on localhost; and the wtcx CLI and the MCP server for people who want to drive it from a terminal.
scope_out: Contributor build instructions and the repo layout — those live in repos.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do I get it running?

title: The Social Contract
one_liner: The fixed yardstick everything else on this site is measured against — for a US citizen, the Constitution and representative democracy actually working the way it was promised. It is what separates misalignment, where an official acted against the contract, from ordinary political disagreement, which this movement does not treat as a finding.
scope_in: Why a movement needs a fixed yardstick instead of an opinion; the US social contract and how it is written down here; how another country plugs in its own; and what counts as misalignment versus what is simply disagreement.
scope_out: Individual policy fights — those are decisions and problems.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Measured against WHAT? Who says you are right?

title: Great American Ethics
one_liner: When a hijacked Congress acts, the damage is not only to the law. Exempting itself from the rules it writes for everyone else, paying settlements and hiding them — each act teaches a whole country that the rules are for other people. Restoring that standard, not just changing who occupies the seats, is the point of the entire movement.
scope_in: What the American ethical standard is and where it is written down; how a captured Congress degrades it act by act — exempting itself from its own laws, paying settlements and hiding them; the cost of teaching a country that the rules are for other people; and restoring the standard as the reason the rest of this site exists.
scope_out: Any single religion's values — the .io door does not carry those; they belong to the party door whose own messaging file asks for them.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Why does this cost the country more than money?
source_section: 20.0 Great American Ethics

title: Problems
one_liner: The movement's ranked catalog of what is wrong — each record sourced, and each one carrying a statement of what the world looks like once it is fixed. A problem with no statable fixed state is a complaint and does not belong here. Any citizen can propose one, and the catalog is meant to grow that way.
scope_in: What a problem record is and the desired_outcome every one of them carries; root causes; how problems are ranked; the current catalog (the Epstein files withheld, the JFK records withheld, Congress exempt from its own laws, settlements paid and hidden, the economy rigged); and how any citizen proposes a new one.
scope_out: The legislative language that would fix a problem — that is fix_laws and good_bills.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What specific problems are you working on?

title: The Rigged Economy
one_liner: Naming the rigged economy out loud, and then proving it with receipts. Who the rigging is for, who pays for it, and how a citizen documents it from the record instead of just feeling it in the grocery bill. Citizens behind every party door already agree the economy is rigged; the work here is turning that agreement into a fix both bases will actually sign — an economy that is ethical and works for the people who do the work.
scope_in: What rigged means concretely, with named mechanisms rather than a mood; how a citizen base identifies and documents the rigging from the public record; who benefits and who pays; the plan to remove it; why a fix has to be one both sides will sign and what it takes to get there; and what an ethical economy that is ideal for workers looks like when it arrives.
scope_out: Party-specific economic packages — each party base builds its own on its own .com door, from its own messaging.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Rigged how, and rigged by whom?
source_section: 5.0 Removing the rigged economy

title: Exposing the Deep State
one_liner: What the deep state, the global elites and the Epstein class have been documented doing — in public, sourced at the door, and never asserted without a record behind it. Where the files are still being withheld, the withholding is itself recorded as a finding, because a gap somebody created on purpose is a fact about the record and not a reason for a citizen to stop talking.
scope_in: What we mean by the deep state, the global elites and the Epstein class; the acts documented so far and the official record behind each one; the withheld-files pattern (Epstein, JFK, Charlie Kirk) and what the withholding itself establishes; and the sourcing rule that governs every sentence written about a living person.
scope_out: Any claim about a living person without a source_url to the official record — never published; see evidence and open_data for how a gap is recorded instead.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What has actually been documented, and where can I read the source myself?
source_section: 7.0 Fully Expose Deep State / Global Elites / Epstein Class

title: US Intelligence
one_liner: US intelligence serves this country and nothing else. It is never a puppet master over American politics, and never the route a foreign power uses to reach American citizens. This area covers the record on the agencies, the whistleblower protection an employee needs to be able to say so in public with specifics, and the rule that citizen data does not get handed to a foreign government.
scope_in: Preventing US intelligence from removing democracy at home; preventing it from acting as a puppet master over US politics; the capture record on the agencies as it stands in the public record; whistleblower protection strong enough that an employee can name specifics and survive it; and no US citizen data handed to foreign countries.
scope_out: Foreign services operating on the United States — that is foreign_intelligence.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Are our own agencies running our politics?
source_section: 8.0 US Intelligence: Prevent them from being controlled by non-US Citizens

title: Foreign Intelligence
one_liner: No foreign service gets to be puppet master over American politics or American citizens. Where it is being attempted, prevent it; where it already happened, expose it from the record. That includes foreign access to classified systems, US defense and research budgets flowing abroad, and paid influencers and propagandists posting as though they were ordinary citizens.
scope_in: Preventing and exposing foreign intelligence work to remove democracy in the USA; preventing and exposing foreign puppet-mastering of US politics and citizens; foreign access to classified systems; no integration of our military, classified systems or data networks with foreign countries; no US defense and research budgets handed abroad; and paid influencers and propagandists operating as if they were citizens.
scope_out: Our own agencies — that is us_intelligence. The mechanism that defends the citizen vote against bots and paid influence — that is trust_scores.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Is a foreign government helping pick our leaders?
source_section: 9.0 Foreign Intelligence: Prevent them from puppet master over US Citizens

title: Election Integrity
one_liner: An election either produces a result that any side can reproduce for itself from the public record, or it does not count. That is a technology problem with a technology answer: open-source voting systems that prevent fraud by design, routine post-election audits, and open gaps published rather than argued away — not a promise from the people running the count.
scope_in: Open-source voting technology and why prevention beats being asked to trust; the guarantee test — an outside team reproducing the official result from the public record alone; routine post-election audits; gaps recorded publicly rather than explained away; and what a citizen can verify without needing anybody's permission.
scope_out: Certifying who won any particular election — the movement does not do that and never will.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do I know the count was real?
source_section: 10.0 Election Integrity

title: No Forever Wars, No Draft
one_liner: No needless wars, no forever wars, and no draft. It is one of the few positions the citizen base holds identically behind all four party doors — and forever wars survive every change of party in Washington anyway, which is itself evidence that the decision is not being made by voters.
scope_in: Why forever wars outlive every change of party; removing the draft and keeping it removed; the record on a draft reinstated against the will of citizens; US defense and research budgets going to other countries; and who profits from a war nobody voted for.
scope_out: A complete foreign-policy platform — that belongs to a party door's own plan.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Will my kids be drafted into another war nobody chose?
source_section: 11.0 No Needless & Forever Wars. No Draft.

title: No Social Credit Score
one_liner: China's social credit system already has an American version. It is assembled out of scoring, de-banking, and access shut off with no due process and no appeal, and nobody here calls it a social credit score — which is exactly why it has to be named, mapped, and removed before it finishes being built.
scope_in: What the American equivalent actually is and where it already operates; why it is not called a social credit score here; scoring, de-banking and access cut off with no due process; vehicle surveillance and remote shutdown as the worked example; and what removing it takes.
scope_out: Our own karma score — a different thing, and the difference is spelled out here on purpose rather than dodged.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Could that happen here?
source_section: 12.0 China Social Credit: Prevent it from being in the USA

title: Laws
one_liner: Four different things get called law here, and this is the map that keeps them apart: the problem laws already on the books, the fix bills the movement drafted that nobody has filed, the good laws that would repair democracy, and the process that turns one into the other. A law is enacted; a bill is only language until somebody files it.
scope_in: The map of the four libraries — problem laws, fix bills, good laws, and the fixing process; the vocabulary, where a law is enacted and a bill is language nobody filed; and why the movement is so careful to keep them apart.
scope_out: The contents of any one library — each has its own area of this site.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What is the difference between a law and a bill here?

title: Problem Laws
one_liner: The enacted laws the American people did not want, were never asked about, and are governed by anyway. Each carries a badness rating from 1 to 100 that citizens vote on, the root causes it creates, sources at the door, and a frozen key — so a record can be argued with in public but never silently changed underneath the argument.
scope_in: What makes a law a problem law and who approves the list; the badness rating 1 to 100 and the citizen vote on it; the root causes each law creates; the frozen key and why a record never silently changes; and how any citizen reports one, with sources mandatory at the door.
scope_out: How a named person voted on them — that is monkey and voting_records.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Which laws are the ones actually doing the damage?
source_section: 18.0 Problem Laws

title: Fixing the Law
one_liner: Pillar 2 in practice: how a problem citizens named becomes real legislative language somebody could file tomorrow. Every draft ships with a coverage matrix showing which root causes it closes and which it visibly leaves open — because a bill that quietly leaves the hole open is exactly how a fix gets sold to the public as done.
scope_in: The path from problem to root causes to drafted sections; the coverage matrix that shows which root causes a draft closes and which it does not; packages of bills that only close the argument together; who writes them; and how a citizen proposes a fix of their own.
scope_out: The finished drafts themselves — those are good_bills.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How does a complaint turn into actual legislation?

title: Fix Bills
one_liner: Real legislative language the movement wrote and nobody in Congress has filed — whole bills with numbered sections, published in the open, waiting for a sponsor. A fix bill is not a law and no page here will ever let it be read as one. It exists so a citizen can point at the exact text and ask their representative why it has not been introduced.
scope_in: The library of drafted fix bills; what each one does section by section; the four-bill Charlie Kirk disclosure package as the worked example; the standing rule that a fix bill is language nobody has filed and no page may imply otherwise; who wrote it; and how a citizen critiques a draft or takes it to a member of Congress.
scope_out: Bills somebody actually filed, and laws that actually passed — those are good_laws. The path from a citizen's complaint to drafted language — that is fix_laws.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Do you have actual legislation, or just ideas?
source_section: 6.0 Fix Bills / Laws

title: Good Laws
one_liner: Laws and bills that would repair democracy — the ones that passed, the ones voted down, and the ones never allowed a vote at all. That third category is the one that matters most: who kept a repair from ever reaching the floor is part of the public record, and here it is written down and kept.
scope_in: The good law list and its admission tests (repeal, restore, transparency, accountability, franchise, due process, speech, purse); the goodness rating and the citizen vote on it; the three fates of a good law — passed, voted down, or never allowed a vote; and how obstruction is recorded when somebody blocks one from advancing.
scope_out: The award a politician earns for advancing them — that is llama.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Has anyone actually tried to fix this, and what happened to it?

title: Replacing Captured Incumbents
one_liner: The strategy in one sentence: elections, and nothing else. A captured incumbent is replaced by getting a party's own base behind the single strongest challenger before the primary, instead of splitting three ways after it. In-party accountability is the cheapest, fastest lever a voter has — the visitor already agrees with the party label and only has to be shown that this particular incumbent is not delivering on it.
scope_in: Why replacement happens at the ballot box and nowhere else; challengers first, and what that means week to week; using a meritocracy so a base rallies behind ONE best challenger rather than splitting the field; running the same play inside every party; and the seat-by-seat view of who holds the seat now and who could take it.
scope_out: How a challenger is assessed — that is qualifications and flamingo. The rosters of people themselves — that is new_politicians and legacy_politicians.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do you actually get a captured incumbent out of office?
source_section: 3.0 Replacing (via Elections) incumbents that are controlled by Global Elites / Deep State

title: Politicians
one_liner: Everything the movement publishes about a politician is an award earned or not earned — never a score, never a grade on the person, and the percentage is always of the award rather than of the human being. This area covers that doctrine, the wall that keeps the in-office voting record apart from everything else, the four rosters, and how a politician or their staff corrects a record.
scope_in: The doctrine that governs every politician page — it is an award, never a score, and not receiving one is not an accusation; the wall between the in-office voting record and everything else; the four rosters and how to find the people who represent you; and how a politician or their staff disputes a record.
scope_out: Each award and each roster — those are the areas below this one.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Are you just calling people names with extra steps?

title: Elected Politicians
one_liner: The people who hold or have held office and left a roll-call record behind them — more than 1,400 of them so far, and the hardest, most checkable evidence this movement has. A recorded vote is a dated act of official power taken in a seat the person was elected to, and it is citable to the Clerk's own record.
scope_in: What a legacy record contains and where each row came from; the roster and how to find who represents you; the two awards a voting record can earn; the pending, for_vote, voted lifecycle that makes it a record rather than a hit list; and how a politician corrects their own record if they are the subject.
scope_out: People who have never held office — that is new_politicians.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What has my representative actually done in office?

title: Good New Leaders
one_liner: The people worth electing who have never held office. With no voting record to read, they are assessed on what they have said and publicly committed to, against rubrics published in advance. Anyone may recommend one, including a visitor who never signs in, and every assessment ships beside a percent-known so the number is never read for more than it says.
scope_in: The roster of good new political leaders; how somebody gets on it, and who may recommend them, which is anyone including a logged-out visitor; what is assessed — interviews, writing, public commitments, background; the percent-known companion that keeps the number honest; and the worrisome-challenger roster, which exists because the same instrument has to be pointed at people we like and people we do not.
scope_out: Anyone with a voting record — that is legacy_politicians.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Who should I vote FOR, not just against?

title: The Monkey Award
one_liner: One award, 0 to 100, for how much a named politician did to put the democracy-damaging laws in place. Higher is worse. The only input is the voting record — what they voted for, authored, blocked, or let advance — and the arithmetic is published so anyone can reproduce the number with a calculator. A 0 means we assessed and found nothing, not that the person is good.
scope_in: What the award claims and the Monkey List it is computed over; the twelve categories every recorded act falls into; why blocking a repair weighs as much as thirty ordinary floor votes; the weighted average, with no curve and no grading against a cohort; why a 0 is not a compliment; and reproducing the number yourself.
scope_out: Anything outside the voting record — by rule that never touches this award, and a build test fails if it tries.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What does a 72% Monkey Award actually mean?

title: The Llama Award
one_liner: The repair side of the voting record: how much a named politician did to repeal harmful law and advance the law that fixes democracy. Higher is better. Same twelve categories and the same equation as the Monkey Award over a different list — and the Llama table is deliberately not the Monkey table turned upside down.
scope_in: The Good Law List and its admission tests; the same twelve categories and the same equation over one different table; why the Llama table is not the Monkey table inverted — a vote for a harmful law costs a repair record several times what it gains the damage record; and dominance, which decides the award a politician's card leads with.
scope_out: Anything outside the voting record — that is flamingo, and the wall keeps them apart.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Does anybody get credit for doing the right thing?

title: The Flamingo Award
one_liner: The award for everything outside the voting record — transcripts, interviews, background, resume, education, public commitments, qualification assessments — and the only award with a state that means we have not looked yet. Earned, not earned, and unknown are three different facts, and the last two must never be allowed to collapse into one another.
scope_in: What the Flamingo covers; the three states and the mark each one carries; why full colour, solid dark red and solid gray-brown mean three different things and why neither blank state ever renders as 0%; the award case; and the per-area drill-in that goes all the way down to a single transcript.
scope_out: The in-office voting record — that is monkey and llama, and the wall keeps them apart.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do you judge someone who has never voted on anything?

title: Voting Records
one_liner: How the public record of how somebody voted is fetched, read, and turned into an award percentage. Every row is cited to the official record — the House Clerk, the Senate, govinfo, congress.gov, or a state's own site — and never to a news article or a convenience API. An unsourced row is dropped, and the drop is reported rather than quietly swallowed.
scope_in: Where the voting data comes from and how it is downloaded; what counts as a vote, an authorship, and a block; how a record turns into an award percentage; and the gaps, which are shown rather than hidden.
scope_out: Assessment of people with no voting record — that is new_politicians and flamingo.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do you know how they voted?

title: Qualifications
one_liner: What actually makes somebody worth electing, written down and published before anyone is assessed. Eighteen named qualification areas — from anti-corruption and constitutional competence to economics, national security and loyalty to the USA — each with a rubric running level 1 to level 10, each carrying a declared percentage weight, and all of it readable by the public in advance so a challenger is measured against a standard rather than against a party label.
scope_in: The eighteen qualification areas (anti-corruption, citizens rights, constitutional governing competence, domestic policy, economics, foreign policy, governance and constitutional law, great life experience, intellectual rigor, loyalty to the USA, management, national security, not controlled and not influenced, policy wonk, public speaking, representation and leadership, US government controlled, and We The Citizens); how a rubric is written level 1 to 10; why a rung measures the altitude of an answer and never a keyword the person had to utter; why a market Democrat, an industrial-policy Republican and a deregulatory libertarian can all earn a 9; long-form video as the evidence base and why a two-hour interview counts more than a clip; the published area weights and a citizen's right to override them with their own; reading the rubrics yourself.
scope_out: The blend that turns per-area assessments into one published number — that is meritocracy. The award the result is published as — that is flamingo.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do you judge a candidate without just judging them by their party?
source_section: 4.0 Meritocracy: finding the best candidates

title: Meritocracy
one_liner: Influence here is earned in public and capped on purpose. Citizens climb a trust ladder by doing checkable work, and the most that work can ever be worth is roughly twice an ordinary citizen's weight — because unbounded merit turns into an oligarchy within a few years. Merit buys attention, never authority. Money and admin favour buy nothing. Staying anonymous never caps the climb.
scope_in: The trust ladder (New, Identified, Contributing, Established, Steward); the merit score and what feeds it — a published corpus anyone can re-derive, verified actions, corroboration, tenure, and accuracy over time; the bounded 2x weight and why an unbounded one ends in oligarchy; merit buying attention and never authority; money and admin favour buying zero; and anonymity never capping the ladder.
scope_out: The action catalog that earns the credit — that is take_action. Whether an account is a believable human — that is trust_scores.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Who gets to decide here, and what stops it becoming a clique?

title: Trust Scores
one_liner: A trust score answers exactly one question — is this a real, believable citizen — and never what that citizen believes. Stitched together, verified citizens form a mesh that can vote, and that mesh is the defense against bots, intelligence services and paid influence operations. Trust is built and voted at the party level on the .com doors; this non-partisan site carries the read-only roll-up.
scope_in: What a trust score is and what it deliberately is not; why it is built and voted on at the party level on the .com doors; the read-only roll-up on this non-partisan site and why it is read-only here; how the mesh puts real weight behind the citizen base; the published policy file that holds every weight and cap so the arithmetic is inspectable; and what the mesh defends against — bots, intelligence services, and intel-service-paid influencers and propagandists.
scope_out: Voting on a trust score — that only happens on a party door. Citizen merit and citizen points — those are meritocracy and karma.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do you know I am a real person and not a bot farm?
source_section: 13.0 Trust scores

title: Decisions
one_liner: Pillar 1 of the product. You record where you actually stand on a question, the platform runs the comparison against the social contract, and a community can pool the result. The answer and the reasoning that produced it are always published together — this product never shows a conclusion without the chain that reached it.
scope_in: Recording a position and your confidence in it; running the calculation against the social contract; the individual position, the community consensus, and the delta between them; yes-or-no votes and policy positions; the paired YAML and Markdown record so software and people read the same thing; and publishing a decision.
scope_out: The value systems that drive the judgement — that is values. The evidence chain underneath it — that is evidence.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How do I record what I actually think, in a form that counts for something?
source_section: 19.0 Community-based voting and collaboration (19.2 Voting on where you sit on the spectrum)

title: Values
one_liner: Pillar 3: write your own this-versus-that rules down in a form software can apply consistently on your behalf, across more material than any person could read. Publish it as a policy packet another citizen can import, or import somebody else's — that is how an ethical framework becomes shared political infrastructure instead of a private opinion.
scope_in: Writing down your rules for deciding this versus that; the structured when / prefer / unless / weight / rationale format; downloading a policy packet you agree with or publishing your own; how the AI applies a value system to a real issue; and the honest limits of doing any of this.
scope_out: Verification of factual chains — that is evidence.
newcomer_question_it_answers: How can software possibly represent what I believe?

title: Evidence
one_liner: Pillar 4, and the movement's most distinctive claim: how to reach a conclusion you can defend when a few links have been withheld on purpose. Lay out every link you do have, name each missing one and why it is missing, set your own threshold for acting, and answer the trap that says because the proof was classified you are not allowed to speak.
scope_in: Chain-of-evidence records; explicit gap tracking with a fixed vocabulary — classified, suppressed, blocked, unknown; setting your own confidence threshold for acting; the AI checking a chain from first principles rather than from authority; and grading a source.
scope_out: Any claim about a living person without a source — never published; see open_data for the sourcing rule.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What if the proof is being withheld on purpose?

title: Communities
one_liner: Where the work happens together. A community is a named, shareable workspace with topic areas inside it and decisions inside those; citizens join it, steward it, and pool their individual positions into a community position — and the app always shows a person the delta between where they stand and where the community landed, rather than quietly averaging them away.
scope_in: What a community is and how it is scoped; the Community to Area to Decision hierarchy; the access model — own, write, read, and world-readable when an owner opens it; joining, leaving and stewarding; how individual decisions aggregate into a community position; and trusted citizens.
scope_out: The merit weighting applied inside that aggregation — that is meritocracy.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Do I have to do this alone?

title: Take Action
one_liner: The catalog of things a citizen can actually do this week — call a representative, add a video to a politician's record, vet a challenger, recruit one, draft a fix bill — each worth points and each logged with a link so somebody else can check it. The movement's scarce resource is action, not opinion, and the gap between reading and doing is where movements die.
scope_in: The action catalog across its four tracks (challengers, communications, organizing, lawmaking); the guided walkthrough that ends in an I-did-it button; what each action is worth, from five points for adding a video up to the historic, peer-verified actions at the top; how an action is logged with a URL and a description as evidence; why the highest-value actions can only be logged by a peer, so nobody scores themselves into the history book; and the monthly caps and other anti-gaming rules.
scope_out: What the points become once they are verified — that is karma.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What can I do today that is not just posting online?
source_section: 16.0 Take Action

title: Karma
one_liner: The citizen side of the ledger, and the one place the word score is used on purpose. Raw points are noise, so they normalize into a monthly karma score and accumulate into a lifetime total; an action shows as recorded immediately and scored only after verification. The History Book of Citizens Fixing Democracy is hash-chained, so a name that earned its way in cannot be quietly written back out.
scope_in: Why karma is deliberately called a score when a politician award never is; raw points to normalized monthly karma, and why the month is the unit; the karma dashboard, the weekly bars and the lifetime number; the verification lifecycle and how a citizen disputes a ruling; the leaderboard, which shows a pseudonym unless the citizen chose to publish a real name; and the Leader History Book, hash-chained so it cannot be rewritten later.
scope_out: The menu of things that earn it — that is take_action. Awards given to politicians — those are monkey, llama and flamingo, and they are not scores.
newcomer_question_it_answers: What do I get out of doing the work?

title: Open Data
one_liner: The movement's public record is a git repository, not a database you are asked to trust. Clone it, follow any claim down to its source_url on the official record, and send back a correction if it is wrong. Where the record is thin, the gap is published rather than hidden — a named gap beats a quiet one, everywhere in this project.
scope_in: The data repo and how it is laid out; the sourcing rule — no claim about a living person without a source_url to the official record, and an unsourced row is dropped and the drop reported; provenance trails for every download; how a citizen proposes a correction, and why a decline has to state a reason the author can read; coverage and the gaps we publish rather than hide; and what the movement deliberately does not collect.
scope_out: The analysis built on top of the data — those are the topic areas above.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Where does all this come from, and can I check it myself?

title: AI
one_liner: What the AI is allowed to do here, what it is never allowed to decide, and the hard rules the build itself enforces. The AI reads, rates, and checks whether a chain of reasoning holds from first principles. Every number that reaches a page is computed in ordinary arithmetic, and a human signs off before anything is published about a named person.
scope_in: AI as a verifier of reasoning rather than an oracle; checking a chain from first principles instead of from authority; assessing transcripts against a rubric that was published first; the advisory-only pass that never awards anything on its own; what a human must always sign off; and the hard rules, including the one saying this codebase never downloads media, enforced by a test that fails the build.
scope_out: Value systems themselves — that is values. The rubrics the AI reads against — that is qualifications.
newcomer_question_it_answers: Is an AI deciding my politics?

title: Repos
one_liner: Every repository the movement runs, what is inside each one, and how to stand the whole thing up on your own machine. The code is open so that nobody has to take the movement's word for anything — including the movement itself, which is the thing that stops us from ever becoming the censor.
scope_in: The repo map — the app (backend, frontend, shared, the wtcx CLI, the MCP server), the open data record, this website, and the paired social network; the licenses; how to contribute code, data, or a correction; running your own instance; and what stops the movement from becoming a gatekeeper.
scope_out: Using the hosted product without building anything — that is get_started.

title: One App, Four Doors
one_liner: How this non-partisan site relates to WeCitizensR.com, WeCitizensD.com, WeCitizensL.com and WeCitizensSocialism.com. One app, one data record, one award pipeline, five front doors. Each door speaks to its own audience in its own voice, none is written to mirror another, and every door names the other three rather than pretending they are not there.

scope_out: The messaging of any single party door — that is written on that door, from that door's own messaging file, and owes nothing to the other three.

title: We The Citizens R

scope_in: What the WeCitizensR.com edition is and why it exists; the three-column seat block (the incumbent in office, the best Republican challenger, and always the strongest challenger for that seat from any other party); how the edition finds the seats you actually vote on; what this door stands for, drawn from marketing/messaging/republicans.md, which is primary for it; and the funnel into app.WeTheCitizens.io.
scope_out: Award arithmetic (monkey, llama, flamingo), which is computed once and party-blind; the reasoning engine, values and evidence chains, which live only in the main app; fundraising, donations and campaign coordination, which no door carries; and anything that characterizes a party rather than a person and a vote.
